title: Common CAS Mistakes Students Make in Their First…
summary: Avoid common CAS mistakes in your first IB term with clear guidance on reflections, evidence, learning outcomes, balanced experiences, and project planning.
body_markdown:
The most **common CAS mistakes students make** in their first term are postponing documentation, treating CAS as an hours checklist, overcommitting, writing descriptive reflections, and misunderstanding the CAS project. These problems are manageable early in DP1 but become harder to repair once academic deadlines intensify.


CAS is not numerically graded, but it is a required part of the Diploma Programme core. Students must participate regularly, maintain a portfolio, complete at least one collaborative CAS project, and provide evidence for the **seven CAS learning outcomes** . This guide explains how to establish those foundations during September-November.


### What CAS requires across the Diploma Programme


The[official IB overview of creativity, activity, service](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/creativity-activity-and-service/) defines three strands:


- **Creativity:** exploring and extending ideas that lead to an original or interpretive product or performance.
- **Activity:** physical exertion contributing to a healthy lifestyle.
- **Service:** collaborative and reciprocal engagement with a community in response to an authentic need.


CAS normally continues for at least **18 months** , with regular engagement and a reasonable balance among the strands. Completion depends on evidence of the learning outcomes, not a universal number of hours. Schools may set local checkpoints, deadlines, or documentation procedures, so distinguish **IB requirements** from school-specific rules.


The[official CAS subject brief](https://www.ibo.org/contentassets/5895a05412144fe890312bad52b17044/cas-2016-english-1st-final-web.pdf) explains that the portfolio records experiences, reflections, and supporting evidence. Although it receives no numerical mark, your school uses it to determine whether you completed CAS.


### The most common CAS mistakes students make


### Waiting for the perfect experience


CAS experiences do not need to be international, unusual, or large-scale. A sustained running programme, school publication, music arrangement, or weekly tutoring commitment can support meaningful learning when it involves purpose, challenge, and reflection.


Begin with one or two manageable experiences that fit your timetable. You can adjust them after learning what is sustainable.


### Treating CAS as an hours competition


Hours may help record participation, especially if your school requests them, but they do not prove learning. Attendance without evidence of planning, challenge, decision-making, or development creates a weak portfolio.


Ask what you hope to achieve, which learning outcome genuinely applies, and what evidence could demonstrate your progress. For further clarification, see[how CAS is marked in the IB Diploma](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-is-cas-marked) .


### Joining too many activities


Students sometimes register for numerous clubs, sports, and service opportunities before understanding the demands of six subjects, TOK, and the Extended Essay. A stronger first-term plan uses **two or three sustainable anchor experiences** .


Depth makes it easier to demonstrate perseverance, skill development, and reflection over time. If scheduling is difficult, use a realistic approach to[balancing CAS with academic work](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/balancing-cas-with-real-life) .


### Assuming every extracurricular activity counts


An activity may be worthwhile without qualifying as an appropriate CAS experience. Passive attendance, routine obligations, or experiences without meaningful personal engagement may not satisfy your school's expectations.


Before committing, explain your role, goal, proposed strand, and possible learning outcomes to your coordinator. Approval procedures vary, so early confirmation is safer than retrospective justification.


### Writing descriptions instead of reflections


“I attended football practice and completed several drills” records an event but says little about learning. Effective reflection examines a difficulty, decision, changed assumption, emotional response, or next step.


Use these prompts:


1. What significant moment occurred?
2. What was difficult or unexpected?
3. How did I respond, and why?
4. What did this reveal about me?
5. What will I change next time?


The guide to[what coordinators want in CAS reflections](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-cas-reflections-what-coordinators-want) provides practical examples. Reflections need not be long essays after every session unless your school requires that format.


### Postponing evidence and forcing learning outcomes


Delayed documentation produces vague reflections and missing photographs, drafts, schedules, feedback, or meeting notes. After a significant session, save one relevant artefact and write a short note while the details remain fresh. RevisionDojo's guide to[strengthening CAS documentation](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/using-revisiondojo-to-strengthen-ib-cas-reflection-and-documentation) offers a repeatable process.


Do not claim every learning outcome for every activity. Select only outcomes supported by your evidence. Across the complete programme, however, you must provide evidence for **all seven outcomes at least once** .


### Confusing an experience with the CAS project


A CAS experience may be individual or collaborative, short or sustained. The required **CAS project** is collaborative, consists of sequential experiences, and lasts at least one month. It may involve one, two, or all three strands.


The[official CAS project guidance](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/creativity-activity-and-service/cas-projects/) emphasizes initiative, perseverance, collaboration, problem-solving, and decision-making. You may not need to begin the project in your first term unless your school requires it, but this is a sensible time to investigate needs and identify collaborators. Review the distinction between a[CAS project and CAS experience](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-counts-as-a-cas-project-vs-a-cas-experience) before labelling your work.


### Planning service without investigating need


Service should respond to an authentic need and respect the community's dignity, autonomy, and perspective. Before organizing a donation drive, for example, ask the community partner what is needed, whether storage exists, and how items should be collected. Investigation prevents waste and creates stronger evidence of planning and ethical decision-making.


### A practical September-November CAS plan


This is a recommended routine, not an official IB deadline schedule.


Period Practical priorities Evidence to retain


September Learn school procedures and begin 1-2 sustainable experiences Goals, approvals, schedules, baseline evidence


October Participate regularly and reflect on meaningful moments Dated reflections, drafts, photographs, feedback


November Review workload and explore a collaborative project Progress evidence, meeting notes, project outline


By November, aim for a reliable routine rather than a completed programme. You should understand where documentation belongs, maintain at least one sustained commitment, and recognize how authentic learning outcomes emerge.


### First-term CAS checklist


Check that you have:


- Read your school's CAS instructions.
- Chosen experiences that fit at least one strand.
- Created a sustainable weekly commitment.
- Stored dated evidence promptly.
- Reflected on decisions, learning, or change.
- Discussed local deadlines and approvals.
- Begun considering project ideas and collaborators.


If you are behind, document a recent meaningful experience, contact your coordinator, and establish a small weekly routine. Never invent retrospective details.


### Conclusion


Avoiding common first-term CAS mistakes requires consistency rather than an impressive list of activities. Choose manageable experiences, confirm school procedures, collect evidence promptly, reflect honestly, and investigate your collaborative project early.


RevisionDojo's[CAS reflection guidance](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/10-powerful-tips-to-write-a-cas-reflection-that-stands-out-in-2025) can help structure this routine. Use it to prompt personal thinking while keeping every final reflection accurate and grounded in your own experience.
